title: The Loss of Friends (Frame)
full_text:
In the southern city of Mahilaropya, there lived a wealthy and enterprising merchant named Vardhamanaka. Observing that even abundant gold diminishes when spent without being increased, he loaded two sturdy bullocks, named Sanjivaka and Nandaka, with rich merchandise and set out on the highway toward Kashmir to trade. As the heavy caravan wound through the dense, tangled jungle of the Vindhya mountains, Sanjivaka stumbled in a muddy ravine, fractured his fetlock, and collapsed in agony beneath the yoke.

Vardhamanaka wept over his faithful beast, but because the forest swarmed with tigers and leopards, his drivers urged him to press forward. Leaving hired men with grass and water to guard the bull, the merchant promised to return. Yet the frightened servants soon abandoned the bull and fled after the caravan, lying to their master that Sanjivaka had died.

Left alone in the wilderness, Sanjivaka did not despair. Licking his wounds, he cropped the luscious emerald grass near the sacred Yamuna river, drank the cool sweet water of mountain brooks, and slowly regained his strength. Within months, he grew as massive and sleek as a mountain cloud, his sharp horns polished like obsidian, and in the sheer joy of vigor, he would paw the earth and bellow with a roar that echoed through the hills like thunder.

Now in that same forest ruled a fierce and mighty lion named Pingalaka, sovereign of all four-footed beasts. Accompanied by his fierce retinue, Pingalaka went down to the river to drink, when suddenly Sanjivaka's thunderous bellow reverberated across the water. Having never heard the bellowing of a bull in the wild, the lion was seized with terror, suspecting that some colossal and supernatural creature had entered his realm. Concealing his dread, Pingalaka crouched beneath a banyan tree, refusing to hunt or stir.

Among the lion's courtiers were two discarded, impoverished jackals named Damanaka and Karataka, sons of the king's former prime minister. Observing their monarch's uneasy posture, Damanaka, who burned with ambitious cunning, whispered to Karataka: 'Look at our royal master! He sits paralyzed with fear, having forsaken the hunt. Let us discover the cause of his dread; by dispelling his terror, we shall regain our lost standing at court.'

Karataka cautioned his brother: 'Why interfere in affairs that do not concern us? He who meddles in business not his own comes to grief, like the monkey who pulled the wedge!'

Yet Damanaka refused to listen. Approaching Pingalaka with humble prostrations, he won the lion's confidence and learned of the mysterious bellow. Boldly offering to investigate, Damanaka trotted into the forest and encountered Sanjivaka. With honeyed words, the cunning jackal convinced the noble bull that King Pingalaka was a just and generous sovereign who desired his friendship. Bringing Sanjivaka to the court under a solemn pledge of safety, Damanaka introduced the two.

Upon meeting, Pingalaka and Sanjivaka recognized each other's noble nature and formed an intimate alliance. Day and night, the lion listened to the bull's profound discourses on statecraft, philosophy, and ethics, neglecting his carnivorous retinue and refusing to kill prey.

Seeing themselves starved and ignored, Damanaka's cunning turned to malice. Resolving to sunder their affection, he began whispering poison into Pingalaka's ear, claiming that Sanjivaka secretly conspired to usurp the throne, while simultaneously warning Sanjivaka that Pingalaka hungered for bull's flesh. Through deceitful slanders, the villainous jackal incited both friends to mortal combat, ending in the tragic death of the innocent Sanjivaka. As Vishnu Sharma warned:
"Even the firmest friendship that was forged with vows of gold
Will shatter into pieces when malicious tales are told;
A whisper in a jealous ear turns brother against brother,
Until the dearest companions destroy and slay each other."
moral: A friendship formed without prudence can easily be poisoned by wicked counselors who seek their own profit.

title: The Wedge-Pulling Monkey
full_text:
In the outskirts of a flourishing town, a wealthy merchant began the construction of an expansive temple dedicated to the welfare of travelers. Skilled carpenters, sawyers, and masons worked daily upon the site, hewing giant trunks of sal and teak into pillars, beams, and decorative cornices.

One sweltering noon, the master woodcutters were sawing halfway through a colossal timber log. To prevent the heavy cleft from snapping shut and binding the iron saw blade while they went to the nearby grove to eat their midday meal of rice and curds, the chief carpenter drove a stout, tapered wedge of khadira wood firmly into the open split.

Shortly after the workmen departed, a troop of wild, mischievous monkeys that inhabited the temple groves swung down from the branches to explore the abandoned construction site. They leaped upon the scaffolding, overturned baskets of lime, and rolled the iron chisels across the flagstones.

Among them was a young, reckless, and intensely curious monkey who could never let anything rest. Seeing the immense split log lying upon the ground, he hopped onto it, straddling the timber right over the open seam. His eyes fastened upon the wooden wedge projecting between the two halves.

'What a strange peg!' chattered the foolish creature. 'Why did those two-legged builders hammer it so tightly between these logs? I must discover what happens when it is loosened!'

Ignoring the uneasy silence of the clearing and his companions' warnings, the meddlesome monkey gripped the stout wedge with both hands, bracing his feet against the timber. He pulled, wrenched, and tugged with all his might. The wedge creaked, loosened slightly, and gave way.

In that instant, the enormous tension of the split log released with the force of an iron spring. The two massive halves slammed shut with a sickening thud, trapping the wretched monkey by his tail and legs. He shrieked in agony, unable to free himself, and perished miserably before the carpenters returned from their meal.

Relating this tale to his ambitious brother Damanaka, the wise jackal Karataka observed:
"He who thrusts his hand into a cleft he did not make,
And meddles in another's work for idle curiosity's sake,
Shall find the trap spring shut upon his folly and his pride,
Like the reckless forest monkey who pulled the wedge and died."
moral: He who meddles in affairs that do not concern him invites swift and certain disaster.

title: The Jackal and the War-Drum
full_text:
A famished jackal named Gomukha wandered across a barren plateau in search of food. His ribs showed through his matted hide, and his tongue hung parched from his jaws. As twilight gathered, he stumbled upon an old, abandoned battlefield where an army had encamped weeks before.

Suddenly, a deep, booming roar echoed through the thickets: 'DUM-DUM-DUM!' The hollow, menacing sound reverberated against the rocks like the footsteps of a colossal monster.

Gomukha's heart leaped into his throat. He tucked his tail between his trembling legs and turned to flee, whimpering in terror: 'Alas! What gigantic demon dwells in this wasteland? If I stay, he will swallow me in a single gulp!'

Yet as he took three panicked bounds, his natural cunning halted him. 'A brave soul,' thought the jackal, 'does not abandon his ground without discovering the truth. Let me examine the source of this frightful thunder before I surrender my hunting ground.'

Crawling cautiously on his belly through the tall, dry grass, Gomukha crept toward the sound. Parting the thorny bushes with his nose, he beheld a large military war-drum, discarded by soldiers beneath an overhanging creepers-laden banyan tree. Whenever the wind blew strong gusts across the ridge, the hanging wild vines whipped across the taut leather drumhead, producing the deep, resonant booming that shook the valley.

Realizing that the monster was nothing more than hollow wood and stretched cowhide, Gomukha chuckled at his foolish terror. He trotted boldly to the drum and thought: 'Surely an instrument that bellows with such an enormous voice must be filled with rich fat and succulent meat!'

He gnawed eagerly through the tough rawhide skin and squeezed his head inside the cavity. To his disappointment, he found nothing within except hollow air and dry wooden ribs. Yet his courage had conquered panic, and wandering nearby, he discovered carcasses left behind by the army, feasting till dawn.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"A hollow voice that shakes the hill may hide an empty frame;
The wise investigate the sound before they shrink in shame;
For he who flees a phantom noise before the truth is known
Surrenders fortune to the wind and starves in fear alone."
moral: Do not be terrified by loud sounds; investigate the source before you run in fear.

title: Vetala Story 1: The Prince Who Married Four Wives
full_text:
Under the pitch-black canopy of a stormy midnight, King Vikramaditya strode fearlessly through the terrifying cremation ground of Ujjayini. Howling winds tore through the cremation pyres, while ghouls, jackals, and screaming spirits danced amidst the smoking embers. Reaching the ancient, gnarled shispa tree, the valiant monarch saw a lifeless corpse hanging upside-down from a high bough.

Unsheathing his sword, Vikramaditya climbed the trunk, cut the rope, and hauled the heavy corpse across his broad shoulders.

Instantly, the mysterious spirit Vetala animated the dead frame, cackling with eerie amusement: 'O King Vikram! You toil through this dreadful graveyard with tireless courage! To lighten your dark journey, listen to this tale of passion and subtle wit!'

In the city of Varanasi lived Prince Vajramukha and his inseparable companion, Buddhi-sharira, the son of the prime minister. While hunting in a dense forest, the prince came upon an expansive lotus pool where Princess Padmavati of Kalinga was bathing with her maidens. Her beauty was like the radiant full moon rising over dark waters, and in that single heartbeat, the prince fell helplessly in love.

Seeing the prince gazing upon her from the bank, the clever princess did not speak a word. Instead, she took a lotus flower from her hair, touched it to her ear, bit the petals with her small white teeth, placed the flower beneath her foot, and pressed it against her heart, before mounting her palanquin and vanishing into the forest.

Returning to his encampment, Prince Vajramukha took to his bed, weeping in despair, unable to comprehend the mysterious gestures.

Buddhi-sharira, however, smiled: 'Grieve not, prince! Her gestures were a secret letter in the language of signs! By touching the lotus to her ear, she revealed that her father rules the country of Karnata; by biting the petals with her teeth, she revealed that her father's name is King Dantavata; by placing the flower beneath her foot, she revealed that her own name is Padmavati; and by pressing it to her heart, she declared that her heart belongs to you!'

Overjoyed, the prince and the minister's son journeyed to Karnata. Taking lodging in the cottage of an old woman who was the princess's foster mother, Buddhi-sharira arranged secret meetings through subtle gifts and coded messages.

Eventually, through the brilliant stratagem of the minister's son, Padmavati was won, and the lovers were united in marriage with royal blessings.

Here the Vetala paused, his cold eyes gleaming in the dark: 'Now tell me, King Vikramaditya: among these three—the prince who loved, the princess who spoke in signs, and the minister's son who deciphered the mystery—to whom does the greatest merit belong? If knowing the answer you remain silent, your head will burst into a hundred fragments!'

King Vikramaditya replied with calm, unshakeable justice: 'The greatest merit belongs entirely to the minister's son, Buddhi-sharira. The prince was blinded by passion; the princess merely followed her romantic desire; but the minister's son acted with pure, selfless intellect, deciphered impossible signs, risked his life in a foreign kingdom, and sought no reward for himself except the happiness of his friend!'

'Your answer is just, O King!' chuckled the Vetala. 'Yet because you broke your vow of silence, I fly back to my tree!'

With a mocking laugh, the corpse slipped from Vikramaditya's shoulders and soared through the stormy sky back to the shispa tree, leaving the indefatigable monarch to turn back and recapture the ghost once more.
moral: Intellect and presence of mind decipher the subtle language of the heart where raw passion is blind.

title: Vetala Story 2: The Three Fastidious Men
full_text:
King Vikramaditya climbed the shispa tree for the second time, cut down the corpse, hoisted it across his back, and strode toward the waiting yogi.

The Vetala whispered into the king's ear: 'O mighty sovereign! Hear now the riddle of the Three Fastidious Brothers of Malwa, whose physical sensitivities were renowned throughout the world!'

In the city of Ujjayini lived three wealthy, aristocratic brothers who possessed supernatural sensitivity in their sensory organs. Hearing of their fame, the King of the realm invited them to a royal banquet to test their claims.

The first brother sat down before a sumptuous feast of fragrant rice cooked with ghee, almonds, and saffron. He tasted a single grain, recoiled with disgust, spat it upon the floor, and cried: 'Faugh! This rice was cultivated near a cremation ground! The grains smell of the ashes of burning corpses!'

The royal cooks were summoned and interrogated. Terrified, the chief grain merchant confessed that the rice had indeed been harvested from a fertile field adjacent to the city cremation ground! The king was astonished by the man's extraordinary sense of smell.

That night, the second brother was provided with a magnificent royal bedstead of carved sandalwood, cushioned with seven thick mattresses of softest eiderdown and covered in fine silk sheets. He lay down to sleep.

At midnight, the second brother groaned in agony, unable to rest. In the morning, his bare back was inspected: across his shoulder blades was a deep, crimson, inflamed welt!

Upon stripping all seven mattresses, the chamberlains discovered a single, coarse human hair that had fallen between the fifth and sixth mattress! The second brother's skin had felt the hair through six layers of down! The king marveled at his incredible sense of touch.

The third brother was strolling in the palace pleasure garden on a pleasant, cool, cloudless night. As the luminous full moon rose over the marble pavilion, shedding its silvery beams across his face, the third brother suddenly screamed in excruciating agony, collapsed to the ground, and fainted!

When the royal physicians examined him, they found that where the moonlight had struck his chest, his skin was blistered and scorched with severe, second-degree burns, as though he had been touched by molten iron!

Here the Vetala chuckled: 'Now, King Vikramaditya, resolve this riddle: among these three fastidious brothers, which of them was truly the most delicate and refined? Speak, or your skull will shatter into fragments!'

Vikramaditya replied with unyielding discernment: 'The third brother, who was burned by the moonlight, was undoubtedly the most fastidious and delicate. The first brother required the physical intake of rice into his mouth to smell the cemetery; the second brother felt a physical hair pressing against his flesh; but the third brother was physically scorched and blistered by mere immaterial moonlight, which is naturally cool and soothing to all other living creatures!'

'Well judged, O King!' cried the Vetala, and with an eerie cackle, the corpse slipped from his back and soared through the night sky back to the shispa bough.
moral: Extreme refinement that verges on physical impossibility reveals the delicate mystery of human perception.

title: Vetala Story 3: The Prince Who Had Seven Wives
full_text:
Undaunted by the darkness or the howling jackals of the cemetery, King Vikramaditya returned to the tree, recaptured the corpse, and hauled it across his back.

The Vetala said: 'O King! Listen to the tale of Prince Suvichara and his seven wedded wives!'

In the flourishing city of Kanauj lived Prince Suvichara, heir to an expansive empire. He took to wife seven beautiful princesses from seven noble dynasties. For many years, the prince lived in magnificent luxury, showering his seven wives with silks, pearls, and golden ornaments, treating each with equal affection in their private palaces.

It happened that an evil, treacherous prime minister conspired with foreign enemies, staged a sudden palace rebellion, and seized the throne. The old emperor was imprisoned, and Prince Suvichara was stripped of his royal titles, condemned to perpetual exile, and driven into the wild, waterless desert barefoot, wearing coarse rags of homespun.

The usurper permitted the prince's seven wives to remain in their luxury or to follow their fallen husband into the desert.

The first five wives shrank in horror from the wilderness: 'We were born princesses of royal blood; our tender feet cannot walk upon burning sands, nor can we drink brackish well water!' They chose to remain in the luxury of the palace.

The sixth wife loved her jewels dearly; she packed seven chests of gold and followed the prince for two leagues, but when the desert sun grew scorching, she wept and returned to her parents' palace.

The seventh wife, Princess Malati, the youngest of all, did not hesitate for a second. She stripped off her diamond necklaces, cast aside her golden bangles, donned coarse beggar's homespun, and followed her disgraced husband into the burning wasteland.

For seven years of bitter exile, Malati shared every hardship. When the prince was parched with fever, she searched rocky ravines for water; when he was wounded by bandits, she bound his wounds with her own torn veil; when they starved, she ate bitter wild roots and gave the sweet berries to her husband.

Eventually, loyal generals raised an army, crushed the usurper, and restored Prince Suvichara to the imperial throne of his ancestors.

The first six wives returned to the palace with garlands, singing songs of welcome, while Malati stood quietly at his side in her worn homespun.

Here the Vetala paused: 'Tell me, King Vikramaditya: among these seven wives, which one possessed the highest spiritual merit and deserved the supreme crown of Empress? Answer, or your head will shatter into pieces!'

Vikramaditya replied: 'The answer appears simple to common minds, but requires profound dharmic insight. While all worldlings praise Malati for her devotion, the highest praise belongs to her because her sacrifice was entirely voluntary and untainted by pride. The other wives loved only the prince's royal position, his jewels, and his golden palace; Malati alone loved the man himself. In sharing his degradation, she proved that true love is an indissoluble spiritual union that shines brightest when the world turns to ashes!'

'True, O King!' whispered the Vetala, and slipped from his back to fly back to the shispa tree.
moral: True devotion is proved not by shared luxury in the palace, but by voluntary suffering in exile.

title: Tenali Raman and the Theft of Wells
full_text:
During a scorching summer in the empire of Vijayanagara, the capital suffered a sudden and inexplicable water shortage. While the Tungabhadra River ran low, several communal wells in the poorer artisan quarters ran completely dry overnight, leaving potters, weavers, and common laborers in distress.

Disturbed by the crisis, King Krishnadevaraya summoned his chief municipal warden, an arrogant officer named Rudrappa.
Rudrappa bowed low and offered a bizarre explanation:
'Your Majesty, the heat of the season is so intense that several public wells have cracked and mysteriously dissolved into subterranean chasms! It will require thirty thousand gold coins from the imperial treasury to construct new wells immediately!'

The King, anxious for his subjects, was about to sign the gold disbursement when Tenali Raman stepped forward with a solemn expression:
'Maharaj, the chief warden's report is profoundly alarming. Indeed, I have noticed that not only have the wells vanished, but thieves have been active under the cover of night. Just yesterday, three full stone wells were seen being carried down the western highway on the backs of thirty pack-bullocks!'

The court erupted in murmurs. King Krishnadevaraya frowned:
'Tenali, art thou mad? How can any thief steal a stone well and carry it on a bullock?'

Tenali bowed with humble gravity:
'Your Majesty, if a stone well can dissolve into thin air as the warden claims, it surely can also be dug up, loaded onto bullocks, and sold to private agricultural estates outside the city walls!'

Tenali then led the King, the ministers, and the royal guards on an unannounced inspection of the private sugarcane plantations belonging to none other than Warden Rudrappa.
There, in the lush, green fields, waterwheels were turning vigorously, pumping thousands of gallons of cool, fresh water from newly dug underground conduits that secretly diverted water from the public city wells! Rudrappa had been selling public water to wealthy orchardists at extortionate prices!

Caught red-handed, Rudrappa fell to his knees in the mud, trembling and confessing his fraud.
King Krishnadevaraya ordered the diversion canals broken immediately, returning abundant water to the artisan quarters. Rudrappa was dismissed and fined double the cost of public repairs.

The King laughed heartily and rewarded Tenali with a gold necklace:
'Only Tenali could use a thief's own impossible tale to catch him in the act!'
moral: Corrupt officials who siphon public resources find their embezzlement exposed when forced to follow their own absurd excuses.

title: The Two Thieves and the Royal Treasure
full_text:
In Vijayanagara lived two notorious burglars, Kalu and Malu, who boasted across the taverns that no lock in the capital could resist their iron picks. Hearing that King Krishnadevaraya had rewarded Tenali Raman with a hefty purse of gold coins for his poetic compositions, the two scoundrels targeted Tenali’s modest suburban house.

One moonlit night, while sitting in his backyard veranda, Tenali noticed the shadows of two men crouching behind the dense mango trees near his boundary wall. Recognizing them as burglars biding their time until the household fell asleep, Tenali did not panic or shout for the watchmen.

Instead, he walked into the bedroom and spoke to his wife, Sharada, in a loud, anxious voice that carried clearly across the quiet yard:
'Sharada! The city is swarming with dangerous thieves tonight! It is unsafe to keep our gold and jewels inside the wooden chest under our cot. Let us pack all our gold coins, silver platters, and ancestral ornaments into the heavy iron-bound trunk. We shall drop it into the deep stone well in our backyard; the water will hide it safely until the morning patrol arrives!'

The two thieves lurking behind the mango trees grinned with greedy delight, nudging each other:
'Listen to the fool! He is dropping his entire fortune straight into the well! We won't even need to pick a lock!'

Tenali and his wife dragged a massive, iron-reinforced wooden trunk into the yard. Tenali had secretly filled it with heavy granite paving stones from his garden path. With a loud heave and a magnificent splash, they dropped the trunk into the deep well:
*KLA-BAM!*
'There,' Tenali sighed loudly. 'Now our fortune is secure. Let us sleep in peace.'
He latched the back door and blew out the oil lamp.

As soon as the house was dark, Kalu and Malu crept out of the shadows.
The well was deep and full of water. To reach the submerged iron trunk, they had to bail out the water.
Grabbing the heavy leather buckets and ropes attached to the well's wooden pulley, the two thieves began hauling water with frantic urgency.
They poured bucket after bucket onto the garden ground.
Tenali quietly opened his back bedroom window, which overlooked the garden, and watched with immense satisfaction. Whenever the water flooded one flowerbed, Tenali disguised his voice in the dark, whispering like a gust of wind:
'A bit more to the brinjal patch on the left, brothers! The jasmine creepers on the right look thirsty as well!'

All through the cool night, the two thieves hauled and poured, sweating, gasping, their muscles aching, until they had bailed out hundreds of buckets of water, thoroughly irrigating every single vegetable bed, mango sapling, and flowerbed in Tenali’s extensive garden!

Just as the first pink rays of dawn broke over the horizon, the water level dropped enough to reveal the trunk.
Exhausted and covered in mud, Kalu and Malu dragged the heavy iron box out of the sludge and pried open the lid with their crowbars.
Inside, beneath the wet straw, lay nothing but jagged granite stones!

At that moment, Tenali stepped out onto the veranda with a silver tray bearing two cups of steaming hot ginger tea.
He smiled warmly:
'Good morning, friends! My garden has never been so thoroughly irrigated! You have saved me three weeks of hard labor. Drink this warm tea before the royal guards arrive to escort you to the palace!'

The two exhausted burglars collapsed onto the wet grass in utter defeat, realizing they had spent the entire night doing honest gardening labor for the wittiest man in Vijayanagara.
moral: A clever mind turns an attempted burglary into free labor, proving that wit effortlessly outsmarts greed.

title: Tenali and the Three Dolls
full_text:
An envoy from a distant northern kingdom arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, carrying an ornate rosewood box lined with crimson silk. Before King Krishnadevaraya and the assembled ministers, the envoy opened the box and placed three small, handcrafted wooden dolls upon the marble table.

The three dolls were identical in every outward respect: each was carved from the same sandalwood, dressed in identical silk robes, possessed the same height, weight, painted smile, and posture.

The foreign envoy challenged the court:
'O Emperor of the South! My sovereign sends these three figures as an intellectual tribute. Though they appear identical to the eye and the scale, one doll is worthless, one doll is of middling value, and one doll is beyond price. If your famed scholars cannot distinguish their true worth before sunset, your court must acknowledge the superiority of our academies!'

The King called upon his senior scholars, chief astrologers, and ministers.
One scholar sniffed the dolls, another weighed them with goldsmith balances, and a third examined their woodgrain with a magnifying glass. None could find the slightest difference.

Seeing the King grow uneasy, Tenali Raman stepped forward with a smile:
'Maharaj, grant me a thin, flexible piece of silver wire, and I shall reveal the true nature of each doll.'

The King commanded the wire brought.
Tenali approached the first doll. He found a tiny, almost invisible hole pierced in its ear. He inserted the silver wire into the doll's right ear.
As he gently pushed the wire forward, the tip of the wire slipped out through the doll's mouth!

Tenali explained:
'Your Majesty, this first doll represents the gossip and the slanderer. Whatever word enters his ear immediately spills out through his mouth to cause mischief and discord. He cannot keep a secret, nor can he be trusted with confidential state affairs. This doll is worthless and dangerous!'

Tenali moved to the second doll and inserted the wire into its ear.
The wire passed through the head and emerged out of the opposite ear!

Tenali declared:
'This second doll represents the shallow, inattentive listener. Whatever wise instruction enters one ear flies straight out through the other. He neither retains knowledge nor harms anyone intentionally, but he forgets all guidance. This doll is of middling value, like an indifferent acquaintance.'

Finally, Tenali inserted the wire into the ear of the third doll.
The wire went in, curled downwards into the figure's carved chest, and remained completely inside, without emerging from mouth or ear!

Tenali smiled with deep reverence:
'This third doll, Maharaj, represents the true friend, the trustworthy confidant, and the loyal minister. Whatever secret or sorrow is confided into his ear is locked forever within the quiet sanctuary of his heart. He listens with empathy, guards confidences with his life, and acts with steadfast integrity. This doll is priceless!'

The foreign envoy was stunned by Tenali’s profound philosophical insight and bowed low:
'Truly, Emperor Krishnadevaraya, the fame of Tenali Raman’s wisdom has not been exaggerated by half!'
The King rewarded Tenali with a chest of pearls, celebrating the truth that character is measured by what one guards within.
moral: True value lies not in outward appearance, but in how one handles the speech and confidences of others.

title: Birbal's Entry to Akbar's Court
full_text:
Long before he was known throughout Hindustan as Raja Birbal, a clever young scholar named Mahesh Das lived in a modest village. One afternoon while hunting in the dense forest near Agra, Emperor Akbar became separated from his royal retinue. Thirsty, exhausted, and hopelessly lost at a junction of three dusty roads, the monarch encountered young Mahesh Das carrying a bundle of firewood.

Akbar called out, 'Young man, which of these roads goes to Agra?'

Mahesh Das smiled gently and replied, 'Sire, roads do not walk! People walk, but roads stay exactly where they are. If you follow the path on the right, you shall reach the red walls of Agra.'

Amused by the youth's quick wit, the Emperor revealed his identity, gave Mahesh Das his signet ring, and invited him to the imperial palace. Months later, Mahesh Das traveled to Agra to claim the Emperor's favor. However, the palace gatekeeper was notoriously corrupt. Seeing the royal ring, the greedy guard sneered, 'I will let you enter only if you swear to give me half of whatever reward the Emperor bestows upon you today!'

Mahesh Das agreed and bowed before Akbar in the grand Diwan-i-Khas. Akbar recognized the clever young man at once and said, 'Ask for whatever your heart desires, and it shall be granted!'

To the astonishment of the courtiers, Mahesh Das answered, 'Your Majesty, grant me one hundred lashes with a leather whip upon my bare back!'

Akbar was stunned, but keeping his imperial word, he ordered the punishment to begin. After fifty gentle lashes were struck upon a cushioned doublet, Mahesh Das raised his hand: 'Hold, Sire! I have a partner who made me promise to surrender half of my reward before entering your gates.'

title: The Crows in the Kingdom

title: The Fox and the Grapes
full_text:
On a sweltering summer afternoon, a sly fox strolled through an orchard bathed in warm sunlight. His throat was parched, and his stomach rumbled with hunger. As he reached a high garden wall, his amber eyes caught sight of a magnificent grapevine that wound its way along a tall wooden trellis. The fox licked his whiskers and grinned. "Here is a feast fit for an emperor," he muttered, stepping back a few paces to gain momentum. With a graceful leap, he sprang high into the air with jaws wide open, but his teeth snapped on empty air, missing the lowest bunch by mere inches.

Refusing to admit defeat, the fox backed up further into the dusty furrow, gathered all his strength, and sprang upward once more. Again he fell short, tumbling onto the soft earth. Three, four, five times he leaped, straining every muscle in his russet body until his breath came in ragged wheezes and his legs trembled with exhaustion.

Looking up at the purple prize that hung tantalizingly out of reach, the fox curled his snout into an arrogant sneer. He brushed the dust from his bushy tail and announced loudly to the listening birds: "Why should I waste my precious energy on such wretched fruit? I can see plainly from here that they are completely green and sour, unfit for a gentleman's palate!" And with his head held high in pretended disgust, he trotted away through the briers.
moral: It is easy to despise and pretend to scorn what you cannot possess.

title: The Tortoise and the Hare
full_text:
A boastful hare never tired of mocking the woodland creatures for their slow pace, reserving his sharpest jeers for the quiet tortoise. "Look at you, my plodding friend!" the hare laughed, bounding in swift circles around the turtle. "You carry your house upon your back and take an hour to cross a single cabbage patch! I am the swiftest runner in all the realm; no beast has ever outstripped my stride."

The tortoise blinked his ancient, patient eyes and replied with calm dignity, "Your legs are swift indeed, friend Hare, but boastful pride often stumbles. I challenge you to a footrace across the valley to the ancient boundary oak."

The hare laughed so heartily he fell into the clover. "A race against you? What a merry jest! Let the fox mark the course!"

The woodland animals gathered at dawn. At the fox's sharp bark, the hare shot forward like an arrow released from a bow, vanishing over the green rise in a cloud of dust. The tortoise simply tucked in his chin and placed one heavy foot after the other, moving forward with quiet, unyielding rhythm.

Halfway along the dusty course, seeing the tortoise was not even within sight, the hare felt confident and bored. "I have hours to spare," he thought, settling down beneath the cool shade of a blossoming apple tree. "A brief nap will refresh me, and I can still overtake that plodder with three bounds before the finish line." The hare closed his eyes and sank into deep slumber.

Meanwhile, the sun climbed high and began its slow descent. The tortoise neither stopped to rest nor turned aside for sweet clover. Step by steady step, his scaly claws gripped the earth. As twilight painted the hills with amber gold, the hare awoke with a start and sprinted desperately toward the boundary oak. But to his dismay, the entire forest erupted in cheers: the patient tortoise had already crossed the finish line, smiling serenely as he proved that steady determination conquers careless speed.

title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
full_text:
Throughout the long, golden days of summer, the meadow blossomed with vibrant wildflowers, sweet clover, and rich grasses. While butterflies fluttered lazily in the warm breeze, an industrious ant worked from dawn to twilight, hauling heavy grains of wheat, seeds, and dried corn kernels back to her underground granary. She bowed her tiny shoulders beneath burdens twice her size, sweating in the heat to store food for the cold days ahead.

Perched upon a tall thistle, a merry grasshopper sang joyful melodies on his fiddle, chirping without a care in the world. Seeing the ant struggle past with a plump barley grain, he laughed dismissively: "Why do you toil so wearily under the blazing sun, little neighbor? Put down that heavy load! Summer is made for dancing, singing, and feasting on the abundance of the earth. Winter is far away; enjoy the golden hour!"

The ant wiped her brow and replied quietly, "Summer will not last forever, friend. When the frosty winds blow and snow buries the meadow, the fields will provide nothing. I advise you to gather while the sun shines." But the grasshopper laughed, shook his green antennae, and continued fiddling his carefree tunes.

Soon autumn stripped the boughs bare, and winter arrived with howling gales and deep, freezing snow. The meadow turned into a frozen, barren desert. Shivering in the icy blast, weak with hunger and without a single crumb to eat, the grasshopper crawled to the ant's snug mound. Through the doorway, he saw the ants enjoying rich stores of grain by their warm hearth.

"Have pity on me, kind neighbor!" begged the starving grasshopper. "Grant me a few morsels of your wheat, or I shall perish in the frost!"

The ant looked at him with sorrowful sternness and asked, "What did you do all through the summer when food was plentiful and the days were long?"

"Alas," wept the grasshopper, "I made sweet music and sang for all the creatures."

"If you were foolish enough to sing away the summer," answered the ant, "then you must dance away the winter," and she closed her door, leaving the idler to face the bitter fruit of his improvidence.
moral: It is best to prepare today for the inevitable needs of tomorrow.

title: Story Of King Shahryar and His Brother

Both monarchs were famed for their splendor and power, yet both suffered bitter disillusionment when betrayal struck their households. For a long time, the shadow of the sultan’s gloom lay heavy over the city. The grand palace grew quiet, the bazaars lost their song, and the vizier walked with bowed shoulders, weeping for his lord’s hardened soul. In that household dwelt the vizier’s elder daughter, Shahrazad, a maiden of extraordinary intellect, courage, and grace. She had read the chronicles of ancient kings, studied the traditions of past nations, mastered philosophy, medicine, and poetry, and stored in her memory more than a thousand volumes of wisdom.

Seeing her father’s grief, Shahrazad spoke with steady resolve: "O father, I beg of you, present me to King Shahryar. Either I shall perish in the attempt, or I shall heal his heart and deliver our people from this enduring sorrow." The vizier turned pale and warned her with parables of danger, yet Shahrazad’s heart remained unshakeable. "Fear not," she replied softly. "Wisdom is an armor that steel cannot pierce."

When she was brought before King Shahryar, she made one humble request: that her younger sister, Dunyazad, might sit by her feet until the hour of dawn. The king, struck by Shahrazad’s calm majesty, consented. As night fell over the palace and the oil lamps flickered against the arabesque tiles, Dunyazad murmured: "O sister, if you are not yet weary, recount to us one of your wonderful tales before morning breaks."

Shahrazad turned her luminous eyes toward the king and said: "With royal leave, O Commander of the Faithful, I shall gladly tell a story of wonder and truth." King Shahryar, expecting nothing more than a passing diversion, granted permission. Thus began the first of the Thousand and One Nights—a tapestry of cunning spirits, brave travelers, honest merchants, and enchanted gardens. As the first light of dawn tinted the minarets, Shahrazad paused at the height of suspense. The king, eager to know the fate of the travelers, spared her day after day. With every passing night, her stories sowed seeds of mercy, understanding, and justice, slowly restoring the monarch’s faith in humanity and bringing golden peace to the kingdom.

title: Tale of the Bull and the Ass
full_text:
In a fertile valley between the two great rivers lived a wealthy merchant endowed with a secret gift: he understood the speech of all beasts, birds, and creeping things. Yet this gift carried a strict warning—should he ever reveal to another human being what the creatures spoke, his peace of mind and very fortune would be forfeited.

In the merchant's courtyard stood a sturdy bull and a sleek, well-fed donkey. Each morning, the bull was harnessed to the heavy iron plow, driven through the rocky fields beneath the burning sun, and returned at dusk drenched in sweat and bruised by the yoke. The donkey, by contrast, spent his days resting beneath shaded palms, dining on sifted barley and clear fountain water, his only labor being to carry the master gently to market when occasion arose.

One evening, as the bull collapsed into the stable with weary groans, the donkey looked over with smug pity. "Friend," said the donkey, "why do you suffer so meekly? Tomorrow, when the plowman comes with your fodder, refuse to eat. Thrash the ground, moan as if struck by illness, and do not rise. If you pretend to be frail, the master will surely let you rest in the cool shade."

The bull thanked the donkey for his ingenious counsel. The next dawn, when the servant brought grain, the bull rolled his eyes, kicked his legs, and feigned dreadful weakness. The servant ran to the merchant in alarm. But the merchant, who had overheard the donkey's whispering the previous night, smiled knowingly. "Since the bull is too sick to plow," ordered the merchant, "harness the healthy donkey in his place and work him without mercy until sunset."

All through the scorching day, the pampered donkey was dragged through briars and mud, whipped whenever he faltered, and forced to turn the heavy earth. When dusk arrived, the donkey staggered back to the stall with broken knees, a bloody neck, and ribs trembling with agony. The bull looked up gratefully: "Blessings upon you, wise companion! Your advice brought me a day of sweet slumber."

The donkey coughed through dust and replied bitterly: "Hear my latest news, brother. As I labored, I overheard the merchant whisper to the butcher that if the bull does not stand strong tomorrow, he must be sold to the meat market." At once the bull leaped to his feet, devoured all his straw, and vowed to pull the plow with double vigor. The merchant, listening behind the partition, laughed heartily at how the meddlesome donkey had cured his own pride by tasting the bitter fruit of his own scheming.

title: Tale of the Merchant and His Wife

The merchant who understood the language of animals lived happily in a countryside manor surrounded by gardens, flocks, and poultry. One starlit evening, as he sat upon the terrace beside his wife, a mother goat passed with her playful kid. The kid leaped into the air and tumbled into the irrigation channel. Hearing the bird's clever remark, the merchant could not restrain himself and burst into loud, merry laughter. His wife immediately turned to him with suspicious eyes and asked: "At what are you laughing with such delight? Are you mocking me in secret?"

The merchant smiled gently and placed his hand upon his chest. "By my honor, dear wife, my amusement was born of the barnyard banter which I alone can interpret. It touches you in no way whatsoever." "Wife," pleaded the merchant, "I cannot disclose it! The covenant of my gift decrees that if I reveal what the beasts speak, my vitality and prosperity will perish." Still, she wept, locked herself in her chambers, and gathered her kinsmen, vowing to neither eat nor drink until the secret was laid bare. Torn between his love for her and the peril of his vow, the merchant sat in despair, preparing his will.

As he walked sorrowfully through the yard, he noticed the proud rooster strutting among the hens, pecking grains and crowing with supreme authority. The farm dog barked in annoyance: "How can you strut and rejoice when our master is preparing for his demise over his wife’s obstinacy?" The rooster shook his scarlet comb and answered: "Our master may be wise in languages, but he lacks resolve! A man must not surrender his life and judgment to petulant whim. A firm word, an unyielding boundary, and an olive branch of reason are the true remedies for domestic peace."

Hearing this, the merchant felt a veil lift from his eyes. He gathered his courage, entered his wife's presence with quiet authority, and told her plainly that her demands were unjust and that no whim would make him destroy their family. Seeing his unwavering resolve and dignity, the wife realized the folly of her relentless pressure. title: Guru Paramartha and His Five Disciples - Introduction
full_text:
In a quiet village in the fertile Tamil country, under the sprawling shade of ancient neem and tamarind trees, stood the modest ashram of Guru Paramartha. The venerable Guru was a man of dignified demeanor, endowed with a flowing silver beard, a round and solemn belly, and an unshakeable conviction that he was the greatest philosopher, scholar, and spiritual preceptor since the dawn of creation. He spoke in slow, grand, Sanskritized phrases, frowned with immense gravity upon the simplest everyday matters, and believed that every trivial incident in life was governed by profound, occult principles of logic.

Yet nature, in her infinite sense of humor, had blessed this exalted teacher with five devoted disciples whose collective intelligence could scarcely match that of a single newborn sparrow. Their names were known far and wide throughout the district:

The first was Matti, the Blockhead, who took every metaphor, idiom, and proverb with absolute, literal seriousness. If the Guru told him to keep an eye on the door, Matti would take off his sandal, pluck out an imaginary eye, and glue his face to the wooden latch.

The second was Madayan, the Dunce, who possessed a boundless imagination and invented elaborate, scholarly explanations for things that needed no explanation at all, confusing cows with clouds and puddles with bottomless oceans.

The third was Peedan, the Clumsy Nuisance, whose fingers dropped every pot, whose feet tripped over every flat stone, and who invariably managed to douse himself with hot porridge or fall backward into mud whenever dignity was required.

The fourth was Asadan, the Ignoramus, who believed he was a master of grand debate, loudly arguing that the sun rose in the west whenever it suited his pride, and confusing his left hand with his right.

The fifth was Mudan, the Stubborn Idiot, who, once an absurd idea settled inside his skull, could not be moved by elephants, royal decrees, or the collapse of the heavens.

Surrounded by these five pillars of intellect, Guru Paramartha would sit on his woven grass mat on the ashram veranda, nodding with solemn satisfaction. 'Knowledge, my faithful children,' the Guru would proclaim in a resonant, nasal drone, 'is the supreme jewel of life. We are not like common worldly peasants who rely on base instinct; we are guided by profound philosophical logic!'

'Yes, Master!' the five disciples would chorused in unison, bowing their heads until their foreheads struck the floor with a hollow thud. 'Our Guru is the ocean of wisdom, and we are his thirsty fish!'

And thus commenced a long, celebrated cycle of misadventures, laughter, and comical disasters, wherein Guru Paramartha and his five disciples journeyed across roads, rivers, and towns, demonstrating to the laughing world that when pompous pedantry replaces practical common sense, folly reigns supreme.

title: The Guru's Beard and Belly
full_text:
Guru Paramartha took extraordinary pride in two physical attributes: his magnificent, flowing silver beard, which reached down to his navel, and his round, dignified belly, which he regarded as the sacred storehouse of Vedic wisdom. Every morning after his prayers, the Guru sat upon a wooden stool while his five disciples performed their assigned duties of grooming.

Matti was entrusted with combing the beard with a broad sandalwood comb; Madayan stood by with a clay bowl of perfumed sesame oil; Peedan held a polished bronze mirror; Asadan fanned away flies with a palm leaf, and Mudan sat cross-legged on the floor, holding the Guru's feet to ensure he did not tip over.

One morning, while Matti was combing the silver hairs with scholarly concentration, his hand twitched and the comb caught upon a stubborn snarl. Matti tugged with earnest devotion; a single silver hair pulled loose, and the Guru let out a sharp squeal of agony: 'Ai-yo! Matti, you clumsy fool, you have uprooted a root of wisdom from my chin!'

Terrified by his master's cry, Matti fell to his knees: 'Forgive me, Master! The hair was rebellious and refused to obey the sacred comb!'

Guru Paramartha stroked his chin with immense gravity: 'A rebellious hair must be reasoned with, not yanked. But look upon my noble belly! Is it not expanding with spiritual fullness?'

Madayan leaned forward and peered at the Guru's belly with profound scientific interest: 'Revered Master, your belly is indeed expanding like the crescent moon approaching fullness. But according to my calculations, if it expands another two inches, your center of spiritual gravity will shift, and you will tilt forward and tumble onto your nose!'

Alarmed by this philosophical prognosis, the Guru questioned: 'What is the remedy, Madayan?'

'The remedy is simple, Master!' proclaimed Madayan. 'To balance the heavy belly in front, we must tie an equal counterweight of stones to your back! Thus will perfect equilibrium be restored between front and rear!'

Delighted by this scientific logic, the Guru ordered five heavy granite grinding stones fetched from the kitchen. Matti and Peedan bound the stones securely to the Guru's shoulders and back with thick coir ropes.

'Now stand up, Master, and test your divine equilibrium!' cheered Asadan.

The Guru attempted to rise. But the combined weight of his majestic belly and the heavy granite stones proved too much for his knees. He wobbled, tipped sideways, and crashed onto the floor like a felled coconut tree, knocking Peedan into the oil bowl and sending the bronze mirror flying across the room!

title: Counting the Disciples
full_text:
Having spent three days visiting a distant village fair to purchase provisions, Guru Paramartha and his five faithful disciples—Matti, Madayan, Peedan, Asadan, and Mudan—set out on the dusty highway to return to their hermitage.

As they approached the outskirts of a dense, shadowy thorn forest, Matti suddenly halted and cried out in great alarm: 'Hold, brothers! We are entering a dangerous wilderness infested with brigands, ghosts, and wild boars! Before we proceed, we must count our numbers to ensure that none of us has been lost along the road!'

The Guru nodded with profound approval: 'Well spoken, Matti! Prudence is the crown of philosophy. Count our flock immediately!'

Matti stepped forward, puffed out his chest, and pointed his index finger at each companion: 'There is our revered Master, one! There is brother Madayan, two! There is brother Peedan, three! There is brother Asadan, four! And there is brother Mudan, five!'

Matti stopped, blinked his eyes, looked around, and shrieked in horror: 'Alas! We were six when we left the hermitage! Now there are only five! One of our brothers is missing! Swallowed by a demon or carried off by a tiger!'

Madayan pushed Matti aside: 'You always were a brainless blockhead, Matti! Step aside and let a scholar count!'

Madayan counted with great solemnity: 'Revered Guru, one; brother Matti, two; brother Peedan, three; brother Asadan, four; brother Mudan, five! Horror upon horror! Matti speaks the truth! There are only five of us! Our beloved brother is gone!'

Peedan counted and arrived at five; Asadan counted and arrived at five; Mudan counted and arrived at five! Finally, Guru Paramartha himself raised his ebony staff, pointed it at his disciples and counted: 'Matti, one; Madayan, two; Peedan, three; Asadan, four; Mudan, five! Merciful heavens! One of my precious disciples has vanished into thin air!'

Convinced that a tragedy had occurred, the six travelers sat down on the roadside dust, threw ashes upon their heads, beat their chests, and began to weep and wail with ear-splitting laments: 'Oh, our poor, lost brother! Which of us has perished? Who among us is dead?'

Presently, an honest village peasant passed by driving a pair of bullocks. Seeing six grown men weeping in the ditch, the peasant halted: 'What calamity has befallen you, holy men?'

The Guru sobbed: 'Good traveler, six of us set out this morning, but alas, cruel fate has stolen one away! Count us, and behold our grief—there are only five left!'

The peasant looked at the group: there stood the Guru and five disciples, six living souls in broad daylight. The peasant instantly understood that each fool had counted his companions, but had completely forgotten to count himself!

Smiling shrewdly, the peasant picked up a slender bamboo switch: 'Worry not, revered sages. I possess a magical stick of truth. Line up in a row, and as I strike each of you across your back with this wand, shout out your number loudly!'

The peasant brought the switch down across Matti's back: THWACK!
'ONE!' yelled Matti, rubbing his shoulders.
THWACK! across Madayan's back: 'TWO!' yelled Madayan.
THWACK! across Peedan: 'THREE!'
THWACK! across Asadan: 'FOUR!'
THWACK! across Mudan: 'FIVE!'
And finally, a respectful, gentle tap across the Guru's broad belly: 'SIX!' gasped the Guru.

The peasant laughed: 'Behold, holy masters! All six of you are present and accounted for!'

Overjoyed by the 'miraculous resurrection' of their missing brother, Guru Paramartha and his disciples fell at the peasant's feet, blessed his cattle, and presented him with a silver coin, marveling at the magical power of the peasant's bamboo stick!
moral: He who forgets to count himself while assessing others ends in foolish despair.

title: The Smell of Soup and the Sound of Money
full_text:
One chilly winter afternoon in the bustling marketplace of Aksehir, a poor, shivering traveler walked past the steaming kitchen of a wealthy restaurant. The tavern master was boiling a giant cauldron of fragrant lamb broth seasoned with garlic, cinnamon, and cumin.

The penniless traveler pulled a dry crust of barley bread from his pocket and held it over the fragrant steam rising from the pot. He turned the bread around, inhaled the mouth-watering aroma deeply, and ate his softened crust with immense satisfaction.

Just as the poor man was about to walk away, the greedy restaurant owner leaped out of the shop, seized him by the collar, and roared: "Pay me five copper coins this instant!"

"For what, sir?" gasped the bewildered traveler. "I took not a single drop of your soup!"

"You nourished your bread with my rich steam!" barked the merchant. "The aroma belongs to my cauldron, and you have consumed its goodness!"

A crowd gathered, arguing loudly, when Mulla Nasruddin arrived riding his little gray donkey. Hearing the dispute, Nasruddin stroked his beard solemnly and announced: "Step aside, citizens! I shall adjudicate this case of high culinary jurisprudence!"

Nasruddin turned to the restaurant owner: "Is it true that this man ate the steam of your soup?"
"It is entirely true, Mulla!" cried the shopkeeper eagerly. "And steam costs good money to produce!"

Nasruddin reached deep into his pocket and pulled out five copper coins. He cupped the coins tightly inside his hands and shook them vigorously right next to the tavern master's ear: Jingle, jingle, clink!

"Do you hear that sound, tavern master?" asked Nasruddin with a serious frown.
"Of course I hear it, Mulla!" replied the greedy man. "What of it?"

"The judgment is settled!" proclaimed Nasruddin, pocketing the coins once more. "The sound of money pays in full for the smell of soup. Case dismissed!"

The crowd burst into uproarious laughter, while the greedy merchant slunk back into his shop, thoroughly outwitted by the Mulla's impeccable justice.
moral: A frivolous claim based on thin air deserves to be paid with nothing more than sound.

title: Who Stole the Smell?

The magistrate, completely baffled by the absurd complaint, summoned Mulla Nasruddin to give his opinion as the resident scholar.

"Then by the ancient law of balance," declared Nasruddin, "the defendants must pay you with an equal portion of their shadows! Tomorrow at noon, when the sun is at its zenith, all thirty citizens shall stand in front of your shop window and allow you to look at their shadows for ten minutes. If you can bake bread with their shadows, you may keep them!"

The entire town square erupted in cheers, and the baker tore down his ridiculous lawsuit in utter embarrassment.

title: The Donkey and the Book
full_text:
Timur the Lame, the fierce conqueror, summoned Mulla Nasruddin to his grand pavilion. "Mulla," boomed the tyrant, "they say you are a teacher of miraculous wisdom. Can you teach my favorite donkey to read the great books of philosophy? If you succeed in ten years, I will grant you a chest of rubies; if you fail, you shall lose your head!"

Nasruddin bowed to the floor: "Sire, it shall be done! I require only ten years and a monthly stipend of gold to conduct the donkey's literary education."

When Nasruddin returned home leading the donkey, his terrified wife wept: "Are you insane, husband? How can an animal learn to read? In ten years you will be executed!"

"Be calm, my dear," smiled Nasruddin with a serene wink. "Ten years is a very long time! Within ten years, either Timur will die, or I will die, or the donkey will die! And in the meantime, we shall live comfortably on the royal stipend!"

Every day, Nasruddin hid grains of barley between the parchment pages of a large book. The donkey quickly learned to flip the pages with his tongue to eat the grains. When Nasruddin brought the donkey before the court, the beast eagerly turned the pages with his muzzle, braying loudly when no more barley was found.

"Look, Your Majesty!" exclaimed Nasruddin proudly. "The donkey has already mastered reading; he has completed chapter three and is now debating the author's logic!" Timur was so amused by the spectacle that he doubled the Mulla's reward.

title: Cinderella (Aschenputtel)
full_text:
The wife of a rich man fell mortally ill. Calling her only daughter to her bedside, she whispered: "Dear child, remain pious and good, and heaven will always protect you; I shall look down upon you from above." Then she closed her eyes in peace.

When winter came, snow covered the mother's grave like a white cloth. When the spring sun melted it, the man took another wife. The stepmother brought two daughters into the house, who were fair of face but vile and black of heart.

They took away the girl's fine clothes, dressed her in an old gray smock, gave her wooden clogs, and forced her into the kitchen. From dawn till dusk, she carried heavy water buckets, lit fires, cooked, and washed. In the evening, having no bed, she had to lie in the hearth ashes, so that she was always dusty and dirty; and therefore they called her Aschenputtel (Cinderella).

When the father went to the fair, he asked the two stepdaughters what gifts he should bring them. The eldest demanded pearls and diamonds; the second wanted fine silks. But Cinderella said: "Father, break off the first twig that strikes against your hat on your way home, and bring it to me."

The father brought her a hazel twig. Cinderella carried it to her mother's grave, planted it in the soil, and wept over it so bitterly that her tears watered the twig. It grew into a magnificent hazel tree. Three times a day, Cinderella went to sit beneath it, weeping and praying; and each time, a gentle white bird flew into the branches, granting whatever wish she whispered from her heart.

The king proclaimed a grand three-day festival, inviting all the maidens in the realm so the prince might choose a bride. The two stepsisters dressed in embroidered velvet, while the cruel stepmother threw a dish of lentils into the hearth ashes, saying: "If you pick these clean in two hours, you may go!"

Cinderella went to the garden door and called:
"You tame pigeons, you turtledoves, and all you birds under heaven,
The good into the pot, the bad into the crop!"

Flocks of white doves swooped down, picking out every good lentil within an hour. But the stepmother laughed mockingly: "You have no dress, you cannot dance, and you would only bring shame upon us!" And she departed with her daughters.

Cinderella ran to her mother's grave beneath the hazel tree and called:
"Shiver and shake, dear little tree,
Throw gold and silver down upon me!"

The white bird threw down a dazzling robe of pure spun gold and silver, and slippers of silk and silver! Cinderella entered the palace, and the prince took her by the hand, dancing with no other maiden all evening. At nightfall, she slipped away like a deer and returned to her ashes.

On the third evening, the bird gave her a dress radiant as the sun, with slippers of solid gold. When she fled the ballroom at midnight, the prince, having coated the palace steps with pitch, found her left golden slipper stuck fast upon the stair!

The prince rode throughout the kingdom: "She alone shall be my bride whose foot fits this golden slipper!" The elder stepsister cut off her toe to force her foot into the slipper, but two white pigeons perched on the hazel tree sang:
"Rook di goo, rook di goo!
There's blood in the shoe!
The shoe is too small,
The true bride is left at the hall!"

The second sister cut off her heel, but the doves sang again of the blood in the shoe.

Then the prince asked: "Have you no other daughter?" The father replied: "Only a stunted kitchen drudge from my first wife."

When Cinderella washed the soot from her hands and face and stepped into the room, the golden slipper slid onto her delicate foot as if molded for it! The prince looked into her eyes and recognized the beautiful maiden who had danced with his heart.

They were wed with grand rejoicings, and the faithful white doves flew down to rest upon Cinderella's shoulders, accompanying the gentle queen through a long life of wisdom and peace.
moral: True goodness and modesty shine through the darkest ashes; patience is crowned with honor.

title: Snow White (Schneewittchen)
full_text:
Once upon a time in midwinter, when snowflakes fell like feathers from heaven, a queen sat sewing at a window with a black ebony frame. Pricking her finger with the needle, three drops of blood fell into the snow. The red looked so lovely upon the white that she thought: "Oh, that I had a child as white as snow, as red as blood, and as black as the wood of this ebony frame!"

Soon after, she bore a little daughter who was as white as snow, as red as blood, and with hair as black as ebony; and she was named Snow White. But when the child was born, the good queen died.

A year later, the king married a proud, vain queen who possessed a magical mirror. Every morning she stepped before it and asked:
"Mirror, mirror, on the wall,
Who in this realm is the fairest of all?"
And the mirror answered:
"You, my queen, are the fairest of all."

When Snow White grew to be seven years old, her beauty blossomed like the dawn. The queen asked her mirror, and it replied:
"Queen, you are full fair, 'tis true,
But Snow White is a thousand times fairer than you!"

Envy turned the queen's heart green and yellow. She ordered a huntsman to take Snow White into the deep forest and slay her. But seeing the child's innocent tears, the huntsman took pity on her: "Run away, poor child!" and brought back the lungs and liver of a wild boar to deceive the queen.

Snow White ran over sharp stones and through briars until she found a charming little cottage nestled among the trees. Inside, seven little beds were neatly made, and seven little plates stood upon the table. Famished and weary, she ate a little from each plate, drank a drop from each cup, and fell asleep in the seventh bed.

The cottage belonged to seven dwarfs who mined for gold and copper in the mountains. Returning with lanterns, they found the sleeping maiden: "Heavens! What a lovely child!" When she awoke and told her tale, they said: "Keep our house, cook, knit, and spin, and you shall dwell with us in peace!"

Three times the wicked queen learned from her mirror that Snow White was alive, and three times she came disguised over the mountains to destroy her: first with a suffocating lace bodice, then with a poisoned comb, and finally with an apple—its white side sweet, but its red cheek laden with mortal poison. When the queen bit the white side to prove it safe, Snow White took a bite of the red, and fell dead upon the floor!

The weeping dwarfs could not bury her in the black earth. They crafted a transparent coffin of pure crystal glass, wrote her royal name in letters of gold, and set it upon the mountain peak, with owls, ravens, and doves keeping vigil.

Years passed, yet Snow White lay uncorrupted, fresh as if asleep. A king's son came to the mountain, fell in love with the silent maiden, and begged the dwarfs for the coffin. As the prince's servants carried it down the crags, one stumbled over a tree root. The sudden jolt dislodged the piece of poisoned apple from Snow White's throat!

She opened her eyes, lifted the glass lid, and smiled: "Where am I?"

"You are with me!" rejoiced the prince.

Their royal wedding was celebrated with great splendor. The wicked queen, summoned to the feast, choked on her own venomous rage when she beheld the living bride, and fled into the dark wilderness, never to be heard from again; while Snow White and her prince ruled their kingdom in harmony and love.
moral: Envy consumes its own host; purity of soul overcomes the snares of malice.

title: Sleeping Beauty (Dornröschen)
full_text:
Long ago, a king and queen longed for a child. One day while the queen was bathing, a frog hopped out of the water and prophesied: "Before a year passes, you shall bring a daughter into the world!"

The prophecy came true, and the king was so overjoyed that he held a magnificent christening banquet. He invited not only his relatives, but the wise fairy women of the realm. There were thirteen in his kingdom, but having only twelve golden plates, one had to remain uninvited.

At the feast, the fairies bestowed miraculous gifts upon the infant princess: virtue, beauty, riches, and wisdom. Eleven had spoken when the uninvited thirteenth fairy burst into the hall, eyes flashing with vengeful spite. She cried in a loud voice: "In her fifteenth year, the king's daughter shall prick her finger on a spinning spindle and drop down dead!"

A shudder ran through the assembly. Then the twelfth fairy stepped forward; she could not undo the dark curse, but she could soften it: "It shall not be death, but a deep sleep of one hundred years into which the princess shall fall!"

The king, hoping to save his child, issued a royal decree banning every spinning wheel and spindle throughout the kingdom, ordering them burned to ashes.

The maiden grew into radiant youth, beloved for her gentle grace. On the day she turned fifteen, while exploring the old castle towers, she climbed a narrow winding stair to a forgotten garret. In the room sat an ancient woman spinning flax.

"What is that merry thing that rattles and hums?" asked the curious princess, reaching out her hand. The moment she touched the spindle, the ancient prophecy was fulfilled: the needle pricked her finger, and she sank down upon the bed in a profound slumber.

The deep sleep fell upon the entire palace! The king and queen fell asleep on their thrones; the courtiers fell asleep in the council chamber; the horses fell asleep in the stables, the hounds in the courtyard, the pigeons upon the roof, and the flies upon the wall! Even the hearth fire ceased its crackling, the roasting spit stopped turning, and the wind died down so that not a leaf stirred on the trees.

Around the castle grew a dense hedge of wild thorn briars. Year by year it grew taller, until it covered the battlements, towers, and flags, so that nothing of the castle could be seen. Across the land spread the legend of Dornröschen (Briar Rose), and many brave princes attempted to force their way through the hedge, but the thorns seized them like iron claws, and they perished miserably.

When the hundred years had passed, a young prince arrived in the province. An old peasant told him of the enchanted castle and the sleeping maiden. The prince boldly approached the thorn hedge; but lo! The hundred years were complete! The thorns transformed into a wall of blooming, fragrant roses that opened willingly to let him pass.

He walked through the silent halls where guards slept standing up with halberds in hand. At last he climbed the tower stairs and opened the garret door. There lay Briar Rose, looking so radiant and beautiful that he could not turn his eyes away. He bent down and kissed her lips.

At the touch of the kiss, Briar Rose opened her large, clear eyes and smiled at him.

The spell was broken! The princess arose, and with her awakened the king, the queen, the horses, the hounds, and the pigeons. The fire leaped up on the hearth, the meat began to roast again, and the royal wedding was celebrated with music and joy, living happily to the end of their days.
moral: Even when malice casts a dark shadow, destiny preserves goodness until the appointed hour of dawn.

title: The Tinderbox
full_text:
A soldier came marching along the high road with his knapsack on his back and a sword at his side: left, right, left, right! He had been to the wars and was now returning home with cheerful spirits, though his pockets were completely empty.

On the edge of the dark forest, he met an old witch. "Good evening, brave soldier!" croaked the witch. "How would you like to have as much gold and silver as your heart desires?"

The soldier halted and listened. The witch pointed to a giant hollow oak tree. "Climb to the top, and you will find an opening. Tie this rope around your waist, and I will lower you into the earth. At the bottom runs a great hall illuminated by three hundred burning lamps. You will pass three doors. Behind the first door sits a great chest guarded by a dog with eyes as large as teacups. Place my blue checked apron upon the floor, set the dog upon it, and take as many copper coppers as you please! Behind the second door sits a dog with eyes as large as mill-wheels; place him upon the apron, and take as much shining silver as you can carry! Behind the third door sits a monster of a dog with eyes as large as round towers; set him upon the apron, and you may fill your pockets with pure gold! In return, bring me only the old tinderbox my grandmother left behind."

The soldier boldly climbed the oak, descended into the hall, and filled his pockets, his boots, and his knapsack with gleaming gold from the third chest. Then he grabbed the old tinderbox and called out to be pulled up. When the witch refused to tell him why she desired the tinderbox above all the gold, a quarrel arose, and the soldier hurried away into the grand royal city.

Now wealthy, the soldier lived in splendor, bought fine clothes, and gave generously to the poor. But soon his gold was spent, and he moved to a dingy garret. In the darkness of the evening, remembering the tinderbox, he struck it once. Sparks flew, and instantly the dog with eyes as large as teacups appeared, barking: "What is my lord's command?"

"Bring me some money!" said the soldier. The dog darted off and returned with a heavy bag of copper. When he struck the box twice, the dog of silver appeared; when he struck it three times, the giant dog of gold arrived!

The soldier learned of the beautiful princess kept locked inside a copper castle because of a prophecy that she would marry a common soldier. Yearning to see her, he struck the box. The great dog brought the sleeping princess on its back through the midnight air. The soldier kissed her hand with tender reverence, and the dog carried her back safely.

When the queen discovered the visits by tying a bag of buckwheat with a small hole to the princess's waist, the soldier was arrested and sentenced to the gallows. But on the scaffold, the soldier asked one last wish: to smoke a final pipe of tobacco. He drew his tinderbox and struck it: once, twice, thrice!

All three enormous dogs leaped into the square, tossing the unjust judges and cruel guards into the air. The townsfolk cheered, rejoicing that an honest, generous soldier would be their king. The princess was released from her copper prison, and they were married amid seven days of joyous festivities, with the three marvelous dogs sitting at the royal banquet table, their huge eyes shining with delight.
moral: True fortune favors courage and presence of mind, but generosity toward others is what preserves genuine happiness.

title: Little Claus and Big Claus
full_text:
In a certain village lived two men who bore the very same name: Claus. One owned four strong horses and was called Big Claus; the other owned only a single humble horse and was called Little Claus.

Every weekday, Little Claus plowed the fields for Big Claus with his one horse. On Sundays, Big Claus loaned his four horses to Little Claus so he could plow his own small plot. Little Claus was so proud that as the village churchgoers passed by, he would crack his whip and cry out: "Gee up, all my five horses!"

"You must not say that!" snarled Big Claus. "Only one of those horses belongs to you!" But when the next crowd passed, Little Claus forgot himself and shouted once more: "Gee up, all my horses!" In a fit of petty rage, Big Claus seized a mallet and struck Little Claus's only horse dead.

Little Claus wept, but he did not despair. He skinned the horse, dried the hide thoroughly, placed it in a sack, and walked toward the town to sell the leather. Caught in a storm, he sought shelter at a farmhouse. Through the window, he saw the farmer's wife entertaining the village parish clerk with roast meat, wine, and sweet cakes. When the suspicious husband returned, the wife hid the feast in the oven and concealed the clerk inside a large wooden chest.

The farmer welcomed Little Claus and offered him plain gruel. Under the table, Little Claus stepped on his dried horsehide, making it squeak loudly. "What has your sack got to say?" asked the curious farmer.

"My sack is a wizard," whispered Little Claus. "He says he has conjured roast meat and wine into your baking oven!" The farmer opened the oven, found the delicious feast, and ate in astonishment. When the sack squeaked again, Little Claus declared that the wizard had conjured the parish clerk into the chest. The farmer was so amazed by the magical sack that he gave Little Claus a bushel of silver coins and the heavy wooden chest to take away.

Out on the road near a deep bridge, Little Claus pretended he was going to heave the heavy chest into the river. The clerk terrified within shouted: "Spare me, and I will give you another full bushel of silver!" Little Claus took the coins and let the clerk go free.

When Big Claus saw Little Claus returning with two full bushels of silver, his eyes bulged with envy. "Where did you get so much treasure?" he demanded.

"I sold the hide of my horse in town," said Little Claus calmly.

Big Claus rushed home, slaughtered all four of his fine horses, and hauled their skins to the city, demanding a bushel of silver for each. The tanners laughed at him and drove him away with sticks. Realizing he had been outwitted, Big Claus stormed back, determined on revenge, but Little Claus's quick wit and cool head continually turned the bully's own traps against him until Big Claus was washed away by his own reckless greed, leaving Little Claus to live in peace and prosperity with his newfound fortune.
moral: Greed and bullying ultimately bring their own downfall, while quiet wit and patience overcome brutal force.

title: The Princess and the Pea
full_text:
Once upon a time, there was a young prince who longed to marry a princess; but she must be a real princess—one possessing true nobility of soul, grace, and exquisite refinement. He traveled across the four corners of the world in search of his ideal, but everywhere he met disappointment. There were princesses in abundance, but whether they were genuine in character was impossible to ascertain; there was always something in their conduct or manners that felt artificial. So the prince returned home to his father's palace, sorrowful and heavy of heart.

One dark evening, a terrible tempest raged over the land. Thunder crashed in deafening bursts, lightning tore open the black sky, and the rain poured down in torrents. It was a fearful night.

Suddenly, a knock was heard at the town gate, and the old king went himself to open it.

Standing outside in the gale was a young maiden. Merciful heavens, what a sight the storm had made of her! Water streamed down from her hair and soaked through her torn garments; it ran in at the tips of her shoes and flowed out at the heels. Yet she stood with calm dignity and declared that she was a real princess.

"Well, we shall soon find out the truth of that!" thought the old queen mother. But she said not a single word. She went quietly into the guest chamber, stripped all the bedding from the royal bedstead, and placed a single tiny green garden pea directly upon the bare wooden boards. Then she laid twenty thick mattresses over the pea, and piled twenty down comforters stuffed with soft eiderdown upon the mattresses.

On this towering couch, the storm-tossed maiden was invited to rest for the night.

In the morning, the royal family gathered at the breakfast table. The queen asked the princess kindly: "Did you sleep well, my dear?"

"Oh, miserably!" replied the maiden softly. "I scarcely closed my eyes the entire night. Heaven alone knows what was in the bed! I lay upon something so terribly hard that my whole body is bruised black and blue. It was dreadful!"

Now they knew with certainty that she was a real princess! No one but a true princess could have possessed a delicacy so refined as to feel a tiny pea through twenty thick mattresses and twenty eiderdown comforters.

The prince took her for his beloved bride with boundless joy, knowing he had found his genuine princess. And the pea was placed in the royal cabinet of curiosities, where it may still be seen to this day, unless someone has carried it away. And that is a true story!
